strengths: Addresses an important question: what multimodal contrastive learning can recover when modalities contain both coupled latent factors and modality-specific variation.
Combines synthetic recovery experiments, including assumption violations and three-run variability, with broad CLIP evaluations across datasets, backbones, and shot counts.
The proposed post-processing is simple and reports useful downstream gains; for example, PCA plus FastICA improves ViT-B/16 two-shot average target accuracy from 32.51% to 37.13%.
weaknesses: The central identifiability proof relies on an incorrect lemma. Lemma 5.1 in Appendix D.1 claims that the optimal normalized contrastive loss is zero, whereas a realizable density-ratio score yields -2I(z_x;z_t), which is negative for dependent latents. Its required almost-sure equality between paired embeddings also forces constant representations under the full-support noisy coupling in Eq. (4), contradicting its uniform-output condition. This invalidates the shared-encoder and nuisance-removal argument used by both main identifiability theorems.

The convex-body proof has an additional substantive error. Equation (43) treats p(z_t) as exactly uniform, although Lemma 4.2 only establishes a limiting claim as lambda approaches zero. At finite lambda, boundary-dependent normalization generally produces a nonuniform marginal, invalidating the stated cross-entropy reduction. Furthermore, Corollary 4.4 requires the non-Euclidean metric restriction introduced only in Appendix E.2; arbitrary norm-induced distances do not guarantee permutation identifiability.

The theoretical justification for FastICA is unsupported. Uniform hyperspherical latents are rotationally invariant and have dependent Cartesian coordinates, so they do not satisfy the independent-source assumptions invoked in Section 5. Mentioning an upper bound of M-1 independent variables does not resolve this incompatibility. The proposed PCA/local-isometry argument likewise does not establish that normalized CLIP embeddings satisfy the convex-body theorem.

The experiments do not isolate disentanglement as the source of improvement. Appendix K changes representation dimensionality substantially and uses FastICA, which includes whitening, but supplies no matched PCA-only, whitening-only, or random-rotation controls. L2-regularized linear probes and dot-product cache similarities are invariant to a common orthogonal rotation, making these controls especially important before attributing gains to ICA's recovered components.

The recovery evidence is insufficient for the claims. Appendix K regresses learned representations on ground-truth latents; this R-squared can be perfect for a rank-deficient linear representation that discards latent factors. Held-out prediction in the reverse direction and rank checks are needed. On real data, selected CelebA traversals and downstream accuracy improvements cannot establish identifiability, and quantitative disentanglement measurements are absent.

The causal contribution and novelty are overstated. An undirected dependency between latent variables does not by itself establish causal semantics or demonstrate an advance beyond DAG-based modeling. No intervention semantics or causal identification result is provided. The identifiability corollaries substantially reuse Zimmermann et al. [67], making the correctness of the proposed multimodal extension particularly central.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. Real-data results lack uncertainty across runs, and the data used to fit PCA/FastICA and select component counts are insufficiently specified. There are also numerical inconsistencies: the RN101 baseline target accuracies in Figure 4 average approximately 22.03%, rather than the reported 20.03%.
